title: Two-colourings with no monochromatic three squares in arithmetic progression
statement: The squares x^2 < z^2 < y^2 are in arithmetic progression when x^2 + y^2 = 2z^2 (the smallest is 1, 25, 49). Colour the integers 1, 2, ..., n with two colours. What is the largest n for which some colouring has no monochromatic progression, i.e. no solution with x, z and y all of the same colour? We have a colouring of 1..22948; the headline cell asks for a 2-colouring of 1..22949 or more, or a proof that none exists. We do not know whether the answer is finite.
submission: Text file: the colours of 1, 2, ..., n as characters 0 and 1, in order (line breaks and lines starting with # are ignored).
score: n, the length of the colouring (larger is better)

best_known.source: Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 10 November 2026: a 2-colouring of 1..22948 with no monochromatic solution, found by an incremental SAT search (CaDiCaL through python-sat; tools/colour_sat.py)

context: Three squares in arithmetic progression are classical (four are impossible, as Fermat claimed and Euler proved; the common differences are congruent numbers times squares), and x^2 + y^2 = 2z^2 is the Pythagorean equation in disguise: u = (y + x)/2, v = (y - x)/2 give u^2 + v^2 = z^2. So this is the Boolean Pythagorean triples question (Heule, Kullmann and Marek 2016: 7825 for two colours) asked for the triples (u - v, z, u + v) instead of (u, v, z); whether every 2-colouring of the integers has a monochromatic one is open, as is the partition regularity of x^2 + y^2 = 2z^2 (Rado-type criteria for squares need five or more variables). Our SAT search slowed sharply near 22948, which suggests, without proving, a finite threshold close by.
references: M. J. H. Heule, O. Kullmann, V. W. Marek, Solving and verifying the Boolean Pythagorean triples problem via cube-and-conquer, SAT 2016, LNCS 9710 (2016) 228-245
S. Chow, S. Lindqvist, S. Prendiville, Rado's criterion over squares and higher powers, J. Eur. Math. Soc. (2021)
K. Conrad, Arithmetic progressions of three squares (expository notes)

novelty.verdict: new. Partition regularity results cover Pythagorean pairs and five or more squares; no colouring threshold for x^2 + y^2 = 2z^2 was found (arXiv, Crossref and web searches).
closest: The Boolean Pythagorean triples problem (Heule, Kullmann and Marek 2016): colour the triples (u, v, z) of the same Pythagorean triples; here the triples (u - v, z, u + v) are coloured.
Our eisenstein-triples: the same question for 120-degree triangles x^2 + xy + y^2 = z^2.
novelty.benchmark: no colouring family for Diophantine equations other than our eisenstein-triples

baseline.text: 22948, held by Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 10 November 2026: the colouring in `refs/squares-ap.txt` (incremental SAT search, tools/colour_sat.py). No upper bound is known.
